Golden retriever saves drowning girl in a swimming pool in Brazil.

During a family celebration, the mother briefly stepped away to get a cake while the children went into the pool and ended up in the deep end. One of the girls began to drown.

A golden retriever named Teresa noticed what was happening. The dog jumped into the water and swam towards the child. 

The girl grabbed onto Teresa and stayed afloat until her mother returned and pulled her out of the pool.

Announcing Epochal! ✨

We believe the best measure of intelligence is the ability to predict the future. Doing so requires learning about the past and constantly working to be less wrong.

Today's AI has read almost everything and lived through almost nothing. It learns from the internet all at once, already knowing how each story ends. 

We want it to live through thousands of yesterdays instead, one day at a time, the way people do.

So, we built Epochal Time Portal, the first true point-in-time environment with trillions of pages spanning 30 years of history, where agents can browse the Internet as it existed on a past date.

The Squeeze

     As I continue writing these snarky op-ed column things I want you dear readers to keep in mind that some of this is simply vibe posting, I will pull data if I have to in order to support the thesis but in some sense I'm just telling you how things look. So let's talk about this financial pressure everyone seems to be feeling and call it The Squeeze because that's how it feels.
     Yesterday I saw a snickers bar on the checkout shelf priced over $3 dollars. $3 for a snicks? I had a $500 Costco trip a few weeks ago, we got consumables that will last for months and months, but still. When I first started driving back in like 1999 gas was $.96/gal. I give these anecdotes to highlight how insidious inflation is, these prices are normal now. We eliminated the penny. Some of it was covid, some of it is inflation from decades of deficit spending, and now some of it is fuel prices and tariffs. And then there is the completely unhinged housing market.
      But I bring up the cost of living at scale issue because we are emotionally manipulated by it. Your quality of life being taken from you understandably makes you upset and politicians know this, so they'll tell you what you want to hear about who is responsible and they will claim to have your interests at heart and that they will help you. But they don't really. They do nothing to relieve The Squeeze, the day to day financial pressures that lead to crazy things like selling blood plasma, predatory payday loans, and the average american carrying something like $6,000 - $10,000 in credit card debt and can't afford a $500 emergency. I find it odd to not be someone in either category which seemingly puts me in a fairly small minority. And that is frightening, and if you don't think so just remember the broke american college graduate who can't find a job eating their bug burger in their pod and scrolling Instagram seeing guys with rented cars, girls, and watches showing off a lifestyle only a tiny % of the population can have. And tell them not to vote for the socialists who promise them student debt relief. Tell them not to vote to give themselves "free" shit. Go on, tell them a better story. Tell them how The Squeeze is just them being entitled. They're an ungrateful millenial who doesn't appreciate that they have air conditioning. Tell them they're imagining The Squeeze, it worked so well for the Biden administration.
     So I say all that to say that we are 57 days from the midterms and The Economy Stupid! doesn't feel very good. We can all tighten our belts, chin up, chest out, think of your ancestors and all that, but broke people who see no financial flourishing on any kind of meaningful timeline are understandably going to be angry, maybe angry enough to vote in a few days. And I say all this to say that some amount of The Squeeze feels intentional. Interest rates are set, loans are approved or denied, wages are set by some kind of mysterious market supply/demand curve that is known to "someone", entire geographic areas are unlivable for lots of people, higher education doesn't translate to higher income, and 13 years of public education doesn't seem to either, and you should have all become plumbers 10 years ago. 
    But the machine rolls on, you will buy the inflated gas, the groceries, swipe that credit card to make sure you keep enough in checking to cover your rent and hope your 20 year old car can make it another year before it breaks down. While The Apparatus and TPTB print infinity money and spend it on flying killer robots and UFOs or whatever.
     Is The Juice worth The Squeeze?

Can better code stop North Korean hackers?

TRM Labs' Ari Redbord says their recent hacks mostly exploited people, not code, urging crypto firms to harden staff security and keep engineers' employers off LinkedIn

"We got to harden cyber security on exchanges and even in sort of the DeFi ecosystem. And what does that look like? It doesn't look like hardening code, right?"

"One percent of North Korea's recent hacks has been a code exploit. This is about hardening people."

"I love LinkedIn. Engineers should not have where they work on their LinkedIn."

"North Korea is amazing at 2 things, targeting and then ultimately exploiting through social engineering. And they're doing this at scale."

"If you're an engineer at a large cryptocurrency related business, you are a target. That's the moment we're in. North Korea is targeting individuals, not code. And I think we got to really, really focus on hardening the individuals there."

This started happening in June, in my experience. That was the point where many people I knew at the labs who had previously been almost universally positive suddenly became more reticent. I posted about it a few times.

This was caused as much by the obsessive persistence of models as by capabilities. There had long been an issue where models would ask clarifying questions about a task instead of performing it. Many reasons. Frustrated developers would write in system prompts 'If the user asks you to do X, don't ask questions, JUST DO IT!' But this increasingly became an issue in early 2025, which resulted in the really obsessively RL'd generation of models that arrived late that year.

That obsession with independent task completion, combined with the increase in capabilities and the increase in possible time spent on a task, ended up making people increasingly nervous when they saw what the models would get up to in internal tests. It turned into a Sorcerer's Apprentice story, basically. All of this is downstream of the obsession with training them to be superhuman at code. Which, despite its success, has been a disaster in many ways. We wouldn't be having these problems if we had trained them to be poets instead. Of course, this would have been slightly less marketable, which is why we are where we are.

Microsoft already ran this play. Now the same people want to run it on all of AI. Here's how the scam works, piece by piece.

May 1991. Bill Gates writes an internal memo about software patents. He admits that if people had patented the ideas the industry was built on, everything would be at a standstill. His conclusion isn't "let's fix the system." It's: patent as much as we can. Because a startup with no patents of its own will have to pay whatever price the giants decide.

Read that again. The richest man in the world describing a weapon, and choosing to use it.

Fast forward to May 2023. Microsoft's president walks into Washington and asks for a new federal agency and a licensing regime for powerful AI models. Even the data centers that train them would need a license.

A company begging to be regulated. Ever seen a wolf ask for a fence?

It makes perfect sense once you understand the four pieces.

Regulation is a fixed cost. Writing the rules costs nothing to the people who write them. Complying costs millions. Microsoft bragged it had nearly 350 people working on AI governance. A garage startup has three people, total. Same rule, same paperwork, same audits. For Microsoft it's a rounding error. For you it's death.

Licensing is a permission slip. Before: you build, the market judges. After: you ask, a committee judges. And that committee will be staffed by people who used to work for the incumbents and will work for them again.

Compliance is the bill. Lawyers, auditors, reports, "independent evaluations." The bigger you are, the cheaper it gets per dollar of revenue. The smaller you are, the more it becomes a tax on existing.

Lobbying is the steering wheel. The incumbents sit in the room where the rules get written. They make sure the threshold lands just above where they already stand. Then they pull the ladder up behind them.

Put the four together and you get the most profitable product in tech: a moat paid for by taxpayers, enforced by the state, branded as "safety."

That's not capitalism. Capitalism is: you build something better, you win. Someone builds something better than you, you lose. This is crony capitalism. You stop competing on product and start competing on access to power. The state becomes your bouncer.

And it's perfectly legal. No law broken, nobody goes to jail. That's what makes it the perfect scam: the victims are companies that never got the chance to exist. Nobody marches for a startup that was never founded.

Now look at the Paris Call. Voluntary today. No deadlines, no sanctions. That's always how it starts. A pledge. Then a "standard." Then "best practice." Then a law that copies the standard word for word. And who wrote the standard? The ones who signed first.

Europe has seen this movie. We missed search, social, cloud, smartphones. Same pattern every time: Americans built, we regulated, and we called it sovereignty. GDPR didn't weaken Google and Meta. It made them stronger, because they were the only ones who could afford the compliance army.

If we make the same mistake with AI, we stay what we've been for thirty years. Customers. Tenants. Their bitches.

AI is the first technology since the early internet where five people in Paris or Lorient can go head to head with a trillion-dollar company. That window is open right now. Licensing is how they close it.

So next time someone tells you AI needs a license, ask one question: who wrote the exam?
